title: Risk factors for overuse injuries in short- and long-distance running: A systematic review
authors: van Poppel D, van der Worp M, Slabbekoorn A, van den Heuvel SSP, van Middelkoop M, Koes BW, Verhagen AP, Scholten-Peeters GGM
journal: Journal of Sport and Health Science
population: Short-distance (20 km per week or less, 10 km per session or less) and long-distance runners in prospective cohorts; searched to February 2019
findings: 29 prospective cohort studies with multivariable analysis (17 short-distance, 11 long-distance, 1 both); risk of bias by QUIPS, certainty by GRADE.
Short-distance runners: previous injuries not attributed to running were the strongest risk factor (high-quality evidence).
Short-distance runners: higher BMI, higher age, male sex, no previous running experience and lower running volume were strong risk factors (moderate-quality evidence).
Long-distance runners: a previous running-related injury was the strongest risk factor (moderate-quality evidence).
Low-quality evidence was found for all risk models as predictors; injuries appear multifactorial.
limitations: Observational evidence only; 'lower running volume' as a risk factor is likely reverse-causal or confounded for novices; the review gives no dose values, only direction.
implications: Justifies BMI, age, running experience and prior injury as the inputs that scale the starting dose, as direction-only adjustments (grade B for the inputs, D for the sizes).
Prior injury of any kind (not only running injuries) should lower the starting dose for novices and low-volume returners.
Because the factors are modest and multifactorial, keep adjustments small and avoid hard cut-offs on age.

Prior injury is the dominant risk marker in both groups: a plan should ask for injury history and use a more conservative ramp after a recent injury (a design choice supported by direction of evidence, not by a threshold).
No previous running experience and low volume mark higher risk in short-distance runners, consistent with a separate cautious novice regime; the review gives no numbers for step size.
Risk-prediction models were low-quality, so the engine should not compute an individual injury probability.
Low volume and no running experience are associated with more injury in short-distance runners, so a structured novice ramp is justified and very low volume is not automatically safe.
No long-run length can be derived from this review; use it only to support progression and volume floors, not a session-length value.
